utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Everyone is present here except Mr. Bourgon. Prosecution is Mr. Vanderpuye and Mr. McCloskey. All right. No preliminaries? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is one preliminary matter that I wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In preparing for this afternoon's session, I came across an error that the witness pointed out to me included in the statement that was admitted yesterday. I wanted to wait until I had the opportunity to address the court and also address counsel with respect to that. That relates to a statement that was made in paragraph 13 of that prior statement to the ICTY, and it is a reference to many people while he's at the camp dying of malnutrition and then includes a reference to a cousin of his. And in fact, that reference is erroneous, and I'll clarify that with the witness on the record, but it should be a reference only to the cousin having died of malnutrition as opposed to many people. If there is an objection, I certainly will address that issue but I just wanted to clarify it for the record so that there is not a misrepresentation, inadvertent as it may be, going to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? I hear none. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One other detail, Mr. President. I think, as I mentioned to Mr. Cubbon yesterday, the next witness in line got here a day later than expected because of a family emergency, and I have finished proofing him and we are ready to go, if we get done earlier than the estimates, we can go, there has been a small proofing note that I've given Defence counsel and I'm -- so we are ready if there is -- if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Vanderpuye, the authorisation or the go-ahead you asked is granted. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will proceed with that. In the meantime, I asked you yesterday, Madam Registrar, to check out with the Defence teams whether they have revised their estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm thinking aloud. I'm just counting or adding. Yes, okay. We'll come to that later, Mr. McCloskey, because I am not that confident that we will be finished with this witness today. So ... all right. Let's -- any further matters? None?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to continue with your testimony. Mr. Vanderpuye will be finishing soon and then I will hand you over to the Defence teams. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel, gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, yesterday we had gone over a number of errors that were contained in the written statement that you signed on the 18th of May, 2000. I wanted to clarify for the record, there is a reference in your statement in paragraph 13 regarding a number of individuals that died as a result of malnutrition at Batkovici. Specifically, the statement reads that many died as a result of malnutrition. Is that an incorrect statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is an incorrect statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Also for clarification of the record. You indicated yesterday that you were in the military from 1992 until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to redact obviously. Let's be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This has already cost us a 5- to 10-minute break. We redact lines 19 to 21 on page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then also line 25. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You had indicated that you had been in the military yesterday in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, were you part of -- were you a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Of the individuals that you had mentioned you were with in Baljkovica on the 18th or the 19th of July, were any of them members of the military or the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when I was captured or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As you knew them on the 18th or 19th, did you know any of them to be members of the Territorial Defence or the military prior to that date? And please avoid naming them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And how many of the five were members of the military or Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two were civilians, three were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: During your journey, can you tell us approximately when it was that you encountered these five individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day before we were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your statement, you made a reference to the camp at Batkovici [Realtime transcript read in error "Baljkovica"] as a concentration camp. Can you tell us what the conditions of the camp were at the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions were very, very hard. We had to work. We had to go wherever we were sent. There was very little food. There was practically no medical assistance given. It was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At the time that you were in the camp, were you at some point registered with the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did come.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You also indicated that while you were there, you had been interrogated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did that interrogation precede or follow your registration with the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know by whom you were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name. All I know that they were from security.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On how many occasions, if you can recall, were you interrogated while you were at the camp at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And on either occasion, did the person who interrogated you identify themselves to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At the time that you first reached the area of Baljkovica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, is there a problem with interpretation or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I think I anticipate, it's line 21, the witness was asked a question about being interrogated at a camp "Baljkovica". The camp is at Batkovici. Baljkovica is not a camp and it would be a pretty important mistake in the transcript for those two places to be confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think point taken. This needs to be -- do you agree with this, first of all, because I'm not in a position even if I knew whether to confirm or not, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do agree. Perhaps I misspoke inadvertently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's take care of that. And is this -- Mr. Borovcanin, is there what you wanted to address? All right. Okay. Go ahead. And thank you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At the time that you first reached the area of Baljkovica, did you arrive there alone or with other individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't alone. There were more of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Without naming the individuals that you arrived with, can you tell us whether the individuals that you arrived with included the five that you had testified about previously that were lined up on the ground and later shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. In all, approximately how many people did you arrive with in Baljkovica before anyone was either captured or surrendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it should be pronounced Batkovic, not vica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did I refer to a camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. No. It's whether with an L or whether with a T.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the one with an L.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not ending with A, just --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise. I'm referring to the area in which the individual was captured, not the camp that he was later brought to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's agree on this because it's important. I mean, you're the one who is most interested obviously, Mr. Haynes. Do you distinguish between the name of the camp and the name of the location? Of the area?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. The camp is Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the area is Batkovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Baljkovica. They are all laughing at me but I thought that was quite good.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think what I'm trying to refer to is Baljkovica which is not the camp but the area in which the capture occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I take it you agree with what Mr. Haynes --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do agree, although I can't quite pronounce it as well as he can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe my question was: In all, approximately how many people did you arrive with in Baljkovica before anyone had been captured or had otherwise surrendered, that you observed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I was captured or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, before you were captured. Or before anyone else had surrendered.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 10 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And as far as you're aware, of the 10 that arrived there, how many were captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And of the six of you that were captured, how many of you, if you know, survive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you say "the two of us," to whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. If he's going to mention a name, then let's go into private session because it's just one name to which he can easily be tied. So let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session. For the record, the examination-in-chief is finished and now we start with the cross-examinations. I'm informed Mr. Zivanovic that -- okay. I notice that Mr. Haynes has -- is standing up. He's going first. Take your time, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't appear to be receiving interpretation. Can I try that again? Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I start asking you questions, I'm going to do my very best to make sure that none of the answers you can give me will reveal your identity, and if I'm going to ask you about names or places that are personal to you, I will do that privately, okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And for your benefit, unless I ask you for a name, I don't want you to give a name. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the camp at Batkovici, the fact that you had arrived there was notified to the international commission for the Red Cross, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about whether they were informed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, when you arrived at Batkovici, did you give your name and your personal details to anybody there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After two days, I think, once I got there, two days after I got there, the Red Cross came and identified us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you give your correct name and details?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The same details that were on the piece of paper that was shown to you yesterday by the Court when you started to give your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you understand that the purpose of giving your name and details to the Red Cross was to enable people to know where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: For example, your government, your army, your family and friends?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when eventually you left the camp at Batkovici, did you discover that people who knew you had found out that you were at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. When eventually you left Batkovici, and you saw people whom you had known from before, did you discover that they had discovered you were at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for two or three questions, please, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Haynes. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any communication from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina about providing evidence of war crimes in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you aware that the high court in Tuzla was receiving evidence from alleged victims of war crimes in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you aware that the MUP State Security Service of Bosnia-Herzegovina was carrying out investigations into war crimes in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And nobody in Tuzla whom you had known from Srebrenica told you of any of those investigations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The nature of the objection has to do with the time frame to which my colleague is referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I suppose you can address that without any problems, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that we are clear, at any time --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Perhaps it better be in private session, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you not think you had important evidence to give about the events you'd witnessed in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. The only thing I did do is talk to people from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, on the 18th of May of 2000, you met a man called Bruce Bursik and you spoke to him together with a female interpreter called Alma Delic. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did they come to your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where did you go to meet them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met in a neighbouring town, in a hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how long did you spend with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure. About a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And during that couple of hours, you understood you were in no danger of getting yourself into trouble?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why I would be afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, did you feel comfortable to speak to them honestly and openly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I felt that I could speak honestly, openly and frankly about some matters. I was not afraid of anything, only perhaps I didn't wish to talk about my private life, my personal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as a result of that conversation, a document was produced, wasn't it, which is called a witness statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you recall putting your signature on every page of that witness statement and signing a declaration at the bottom of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I signed it but I don't remember that I actually did sign each and every page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you remember it being read back to you before you signed it, in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but it is possible that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, do you remember whether you, in fact, made any corrections when it was read back to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. I want to come to last Sunday afternoon, that's two days ago, which you spent with the gentleman over there in a room somewhere in this building. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How many people were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Does that include the gentleman who has just been asking you questions? Was it him and one other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there, and a young lady, an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say about two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how did the meeting go? Did it begin by you being shown your May 2000 statement and having it read over to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you point out the mistakes in that statement immediately or at some later stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I read it, I did notice some mistakes. Now, were they mistakes in translation, well, most probably, as it was being translated. So that would be about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I don't suppose that took up the whole of two and a half hours. So you were doing something other than reading your statement for two and a half hours. Were you shown anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, were you shown any photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just one photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was that of a building or of a person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear this last word.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was the photograph of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that photograph I could recognise a facility; namely, the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was said to you when that one photograph was shown to you? Were you told, "This is where we believe you were held; can you confirm that?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked whether I could recognise the building and where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you shown any videotapes or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Any other written material?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just had to read what I had to read, and there was that one photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on from that. Now, the 39 men that were held prisoner in the toilet next to the wood varnish factory, would they be the same 39 men who were taken to the camp at Batkovici from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long were you held in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about three days approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to say that I think he answered that yesterday. He gave the duration on one place and then another until the very end, when he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wasn't sure that he had but if he had, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you arrived, were the other -- were the other prisoners substantially there? Were you one of the last to arrive or were you one of the first to arrive? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the first to arrive. There was no one else there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to ask you in particular whether you remember two other prisoners who may have been there at the same time as you, two brothers, who were taken to hospital for treatment and who came back carrying envelopes with X-ray pictures inside them. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall two brothers. Can I tell you where they were from?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We will go into private session if you're going to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: please. [Open session]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You now you were arrested as a soldier in enemy territory, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In fact, just before you were arrested, you had been carrying arms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And more than that, you'd had your arms ready to shoot at Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's be realistic. Being arrested in those circumstances, whatever side you were on in this war, the best result you could have hoped for was to be taken to a detention camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean, perhaps you can help us. You'd been patrolling for three years in the Srebrenica enclave. What facilities did your opstina have for the detention of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, it hardly ever happened that somebody would be taken prisoner. Even if they would be taken prisoner, the only facility for that was the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another topic now. I don't want to take too long over this, but can we agree, however difficult it is to work out the days, that you arrived in Baljkovica no later than the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, can we just go through it as it were from both ends very quickly? You left Susnjari late in the evening of the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The following day, you were ambushed in the morning and shelled in the evening, and you might recall the details of that ambush where you were carrying stretchers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: On the 13th, the day after that, you saw people being killed who tried to cross the road at Sandici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And on the 14th, you climbed down some cliffs near Kuslat using electrical wires and you crossed the Drinjaca river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't have been the 14th. No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, would it have been earlier or later than that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: For what it's worth, you said in your witness statement that you arrived in Baljkovica on the 16th. But we'll carry on. After you'd crossed the river, you made towards Snagovo, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We set out towards Rasovo, towards Udric, not towards Snagovo, the same direction but Snagovo was pretty far off from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can approach it another way. You spent at least three nights, didn't you, not very far from Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was it roughly, from Udric and then to Baljkovica, roughly it's that amount of time. Because we were ambushed quite a few times and then we had to go back and then we had to go around. So approximately that was the time it took.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you made your -- I'm sorry, can I start this question again? When ultimately you were captured, you were interrogated, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if I can put it this way, to a large extent, it was a pretty standard interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my opinion is that it is so. Whoever was taken prisoner was probably interrogated first and then they did whatever they had planned on doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you could hear other people being interrogated as well, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not hear that. I could only see people being taken out one by one, to be interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The more unusual questions you were asked were -- you were asked whether you had ever received arms packages disguised as aid in the enclave, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you were also asked, weren't you, why you had not gone to the free territory through the corridor when it had been opened for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They put many questions to us. As for an open corridor, we didn't have that anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's start at this point: Were you asked why you had not gone through the open corridor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that question. I don't think they asked me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. As you made your way towards Baljkovica, were you aware of fighting ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was a single place from Kamenicko Brdo to Baljkovica, where there was no shooting. Every 500 metres, every kilometre, there were ambushes. So there was shooting all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you aware, that beyond Baljkovica, was the free territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. When I came to Baljkovica, a group came together with me. I was in that group. As we got there, we found quite a few people who had already been there. There was quite a big group of people there, about perhaps 1.000 persons. I found that strange, why they were there. I asked them why don't you go? And they said, you can't get through. About 20 of us set out to try to get through. When we got too close to the line, we were shot at. Fortunately, no one got wounded or killed. We went back to that same group up there, and this same group that was with me set out and we went our separate ways at one point. 10 of us remained, and we thought that they had taken that road, although they had actually gone left, and we went right. So that is where we went our separate ways. We arrived in the evening, we spent the night there, by a brook that we tried to cross in the morning. When we saw that we couldn't cross the brook, about 8.00 in the morning, as we were wondering where we would go and what we would do, we were simply exhausted, we fell asleep, and were awakened by gunfire. We were being told to surrender. We were told that we were surrounded and that we had nowhere to go. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you aware of fire coming from, as it were, beyond Baljkovica, from the area of the free territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw the line. It was the line where the Serb soldiers were. Behind that line, roughly three or four or 500 metres away, there was yet another line on the other side, towards Tuzla. The Bosnian army was at that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were they firing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who you mean, the Serb soldiers or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The Bosnian army that you could see towards Tuzla, firing towards Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about the people who were with you, who were advancing towards Baljkovica, were they firing on the Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So, as you moved towards Baljkovica, was there any fire going on at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our side or from the Serb soldiers' side?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: From anybody.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would happen scores of times or more, mostly coming from the Serb side. Because we were ordered not to put up resistance at all. Most of us had wives, children, who were already in Potocari and we were told that any resistance on our part could harm our families who were already in Potocari. Had we put up a resistance, perhaps none of this would have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: From whom were you receiving those orders when you were at Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not when we were in Baljkovica. The orders were issued when we left from Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to see if I can understand this. You arrived in Baljkovica with a group of about 10 people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to have to explain my answer. I arrived at Baljkovica with some people. I don't know exactly how many of them there were. As for where I was captured, that's where I came with 10 people. And the place where I was captured, I heard over the radio, and I said that yesterday, that the commander who was there was speaking with someone. I don't know with whom. He asked what was the name of that place, because he was taking down our particulars, what our names were, who we were, where we were from and so on. He was asking. He had a notebook where he was noting down everything, all the first and last names. He asked how he should write in this place, and the answer he got was that it was Tisova Kosa. So now we know where I got to, with how many people and with how many people I was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was only asking you how many people you arrived with when you first got to Baljkovica. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it was a group of 20 to 30 people. Although people were arriving after me. There were also people ahead of me. So I would say that there were people ahead of me, 100 metres in front of me, that were arriving also a hundred metres behind me. But the group that I arrived with had about that many men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how many of those men were armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few. Even the ones that were armed had some hunting weapons mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Baljkovica, there were a very large group of people there, wasn't there, a thousand or more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And using your best estimation, was that group of people all armed, mostly armed, some of them armed or very few of them armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few of them were armed, because people who were armed were walking in the front, and they reached that place first. They passed through first. All the people that were left behind included very, very few armed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you talk to people in Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did anyone mention the corridor to the free territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly people were saying who they knew, they were talking amongst themselves, where they could go to pass through. People were mostly unarmed. You could not cross the lines unarmed. Some were saying that they were going to the left, through Kladanj. I didn't know the area, actually. I didn't know where you could pass or which areas you could bypass. One was tired, hungry, thirsty, bare foot, without sleep, so it was just the simplest thing. If somebody said, "Let's go this way," you would simply go that way and follow them. People had different opinions as to where to go. Some said, "Let's go this way." Some said, "Let's go that way." And that's how groups of people, 10 people, 3 people, 5 people, 20 people, started going off, depending on what they decided amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You left that area with a group of 20 other people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At the time you left Baljkovica, was there any fighting going on in the area then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: As a soldier yourself, were you aware that commands were getting through from your -- the command of your army to people on the ground in Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify your question? Where we were when? I mean, about these orders, where they were coming in from and where we were?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you receive any orders when you were at Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We -- there was nobody to receive the orders from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you aware, when you were at Baljkovica, of a large -- the movement of a large body of people across the valley to the free territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You didn't see thousands of people walking across Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Nor hear them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because if I had seen them, I would have crossed over together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You weren't aware of a surge of people in any particular direction when you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have seen that before Baljkovica only, that people were going towards Baljkovica, but that was the last stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean, were you not concerned, as an armed man, to leave all these unarmed people behind in Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Your group was armed and they left behind a group of substantially unarmed people. Didn't you think you should stay and protect them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such circumstances, no one was paying attention to anyone else. We saw that we had been betrayed by all sides. It was clear to everyone, whoever was just a normal person, a regular person, understood that we had been betrayed, first by the United Nations because we were supposed to be a safe zone, a protected area. When they betrayed us, no one trusted anyone else any longer. As for what you say that we were armed, an armed person, if there are 20 of us in a group and five are armed and 15 are not armed, it means that altogether we were not armed. If the majority of us were armed, that would mean that we were armed. The people who stayed behind, amongst them I said a minority was armed, perhaps in a thousand people there were 100 or 150 who had hunting weapons. And anyone who knew anyone together in groups of 10, 15 or 20 people, they would get together in these groups, and in every group there were perhaps two or three rifles and the group would have 10, 15, up to 50 people, it depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Serbian soldiers calling to you through megaphones when you were at Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: Did you think, if there was a corridor, you would have been able to walk through it carrying your automatic weapon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would object to the question, Mr. President. I think that it calls for speculation. The think the witness has testified repeatedly that he wasn't aware of any corridor that had been opened, and I think the question simply invites a speculative answer from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think objection is sustained. And I suggest you move on to the next question. Or next area of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already said that he was not aware of any corridor and any answer would be speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The following day, after you'd left Baljkovica with this group of people, you were involved in a fire-fight, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when I was captured or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, the day before you were captured.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Only when I tried to get across the line, in those -- in the group of 21, they fired at us, so we turned back. That was the only time when there was firing directly at us. They didn't allow us to get across.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's what I was referring to, in fairness. Were you surprised by the fire that came upon you on the 17th of July or the day on which you tried to cross the line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how close were you to the fire, the group of you, when it began?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe 150 to 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And none of your group were killed or injured in that exchange?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's about three minutes before break time but this is actually a very convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll have a 30-minute break. That means we'll start again at 13 minutes past 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to move on but I just want to ask you three questions to recap on what we've just been dealing with, if I may. The first is this: You told us that you were able to see the lines of the Bosnian army beyond Baljkovica, you said about 400 or 500 metres behind the Serb forces from where you were, and that they were not firing at Serbian positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you surprised that they weren't firing at Serbian positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not surprised at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you said that when you arrived at Baljkovica, there was no fighting. Did it surprise you there was no fighting at Baljkovica when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That didn't surprise me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to clarify your evidence, as it were, about the whole of the line of cross-examination I've just conducted. Is it your testimony that throughout three days and three nights in the area of Baljkovica, you never heard one word about the corridor to the free territory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- you've put that question about six times already, Mr. Haynes, and he's always given you a no answer. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: As long as the witness is happy with that position, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, can we move to the morning of your capture? The area in which you were sleeping or hiding was an area of very tall grass, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you have no idea, do you, what happened to three of the people who had been with you the day before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what three people you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go to private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you were asked four times to surrender while the group of you were in the long grass there. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Over what period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It may be my fault for asking a loose question but what time -- what was the difference in time between, as it were, the first time you were -- heard calls for you to surrender and the time at which you actually did surrender?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a long time, perhaps only about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And after the first time you were asked to surrender, was there any shooting then, or not until later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you mean yes, there was shooting after the first time you were asked to surrender?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was that shooting over your heads or into the grass itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above, over our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And after the second time you were asked to surrender, was the shooting then over your heads or into the grass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, over our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: After the third request, was the firing into the grass or over your heads?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were firing at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that the fire was directed at the group of you in the grass after two warnings, or after two requests for you to surrender?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And from what distance was the fire being directed at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between some 20 and 50 metres, depending on where the soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how many soldiers were shooting at you, do you think?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately around 20, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you said from all around you, completely encircling you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you aware of anybody being hit by fire in the long grass? Did you hear anybody cry out or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And eventually you decided to surrender so you threw away your gun and you walked out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long you were held at the site of your capture before you were driven away somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, say, about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And during that time, you were held by soldiers who wore a certain insignia, wearing red, white, and blue colours with a double-headed eagle on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well this eagle with the four Ss, the four Cyrillic Ss, where it said "Vojska Republika Srpska," the army of Republika Srpska, camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to see if I can help you here, and I'm going to ask the usher, please, if she'll call up 7063 and go to page 5. Now, for the benefit of the Court, these are in e-court and because they had to be scanned, they've come out black and white. We can in fact show the witness these documents in colour, so I'm going to ask Ms. Kaker if she'd call up these documents in colour, please. Now, on each of those insignia, you can see in the centre the eagle with the four Cyrillic Ss in the middle of its chest. Is that the insignia you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't these.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. I'm not suggesting that it was, but was the eagle that you saw with the four Cyrillic Ss similar to the design you see in the centre of each of those insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the indication that these were soldiers from the VRS army, was that similarly like the letters we see at the top of those badges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember whether this is the way it was, abbreviated, or whether it was the full sentence, the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much but can we take it that unlike these badges, the ones you saw did not give any indication of what region the brigade came from? You see on the first one there, on the left, it says "Srbacka Brigada," doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If it had been written, I would have known roughly what brigade it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Thank you very much. Now, your impression was that these soldiers came from Serbia itself. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was that based on, their accent or something about the equipment they had or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way they talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And after about an hour, as you've told us, you were taken away in a black Mercedes motor vehicle, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, were you taken away by two soldiers whose names you knew as Zoran and Goran?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not soldiers. They were from the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. It's probably my fault that we've got a disagreement. There were two men who took you away called Zoran and Goran; you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called them Zokie and Gokie.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That will do for me. And were you taken away in a Mercedes motor vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They first took me on a truck, a small TAM truck called Tamic, to this place where the line was. There were quite a few Serb soldiers there, 300, 400, 500, I cannot say exactly. They were roasting some meat there on the spit. As we got there some were yelling, saying, "Bring him down here so that we can roast him on the spit." They were asking me all sorts of things. Many soldiers walked up to me and said -- asking me who I was and where the others were, this and that and the other thing. I was kept there for, say, half an hour, 40 minutes. A commander ordered them to drive me to Zvornik. That's when the black Mercedes came. They put me into this Mercedes. I was sitting next to the driver. That same policeman sat behind me but this time there was only this one there. He sat behind me. And that's how they drove me to Zvornik. We talked, sort of. This policeman told me to admit everything I knew, not to lie about anything, that I would be better off that way, and if they ask me whether I should be sent to Fikret Abdic, to wage war for them, that I should say yes to that, that that's better than them killing me. And I said, "Right, no problem." While he was telling me to confess all of that and that it would be better for me, he said, "Well, if they interrogate you, and if they put your name into the black book, you're done." I kept quiet because I knew that my fate was in somebody else's hands and that I had no choice. It would be the way my fate was, and I said, "No problem."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you the only prisoner taken away in the Tamic truck and the only prisoner in the black Mercedes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Amongst the group of you that had been hiding in the grass, was there something unusual about you? Were you younger than anybody else or were you of a more senior rank than anybody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were of different age groups. The youngest person among us was -- well, I think he was born in 1989, and the oldest one was, say, born in 1940, 1940 something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't suppose you really mean somebody was born in 1989. That would have made him six years old.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry, I actually meant 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was there something special about you that meant that of those you say were captured you were the only one to be taken in a car to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was captured, the commander talked to someone over the radio and they were discussing some exchange. Since I said I was a soldier, they needed soldiers for an exchange, so most probably they decided to leave me for an exchange. This man, this commander, who was there, said to me that I would be exchanged. I didn't believe that. I kept thinking about what that soldier had told me, that they wanted to slit my throat and that they probably left me there to have my throat slit. This soldier who wanted to slit my throat asked, "Should I take him?" And then he hollered at him and said, "Fuck you, I'm not saying anything to you." And then he ordered these other two policemen to take me away. I thought that they were going to kill me. When they took me down there, I waited for about 15, 20 minutes, up to half an hour until the truck came. They put me into that truck and they drove me to where those Serb soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to clarify one thing with you. The conversation that you heard the commanding officer have on his radio was one in which he was told not to kill you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just heard him say that I was needed for an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, two questions further about, as it were, what you saw at Baljkovica. The operation that you saw the Serbian soldiers conducting, which led to your capture, was an operation of combing the terrain, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what this looks like to you, because when we were surrounded, we were all asleep then. Now, I don't know, most probably they saw us when we arrived there, because we were so tired, we had had so little sleep that we fell asleep as soon as we sat there, although we could have returned from that place, say 100 metres, 200 metres. Perhaps we would have been safer there. But we were so tired that we just fell asleep there. They came there and surrounded us and that's where they took us prisoner. Now, did they see us and then surround us, or did they set out to clean up the terrain, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Once the terrain had been combed, the next military objective is to clean up the terrain, isn't it, to pick up discarded arms and to dispose of dead bodies and the like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please just clarify that question? At least a bit for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do my best. What I was suggesting to you earlier was that the soldiers who took you captive were combing the area to try and find whether there were any enemy forces still on their territory. That's what I was suggesting to you they were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would object to the question. I don't think that the specific legal grounds that it assumes a fact that's not in evidence. The witness hasn't testified that that was the operation that the soldiers were engaged in or that was his observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I simply put that that was what I was suggesting to him to explain the following question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And at the same time, however, he did answer you that he was asleep together with the others, who were also asleep, and he can't answer your question. So if he can't answer -- if he can't tell you what they were doing, all the rest becomes speculation, suppositions. I don't really --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't think it does, actually, but if you'll permit me a couple of questions, we'll get there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleagues on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please phrase it a little bit differently, Mr. Haynes, and kindly bring this chapter to an end. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you understand the military term asanacija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a question to me or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll ask one more question on this topic, then I'll leave it. You saw a lot of dead bodies scattered around the area in Baljkovica, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And at some stage, to make the area hygienic, they would have needed to be removed, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Limiting this to the Baljkovica area, how many dead bodies do you think you saw in the three days that you were there in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were bodies everywhere. As for those killed, I think there were fewer killed there than in the area around Konjevic Polje, Sandici, Kamenica. All the people who were wounded there or were killed, because the distance wasn't great, so once the breakthrough was made, the corridor was broken through, which was done by armed soldiers. They managed to carry across or bring across all those who had been wounded, so that's how they were saved. So in that area, on that terrain, I saw perhaps about 100 to 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I've only got one or two more questions and then I'm finished. When you arrived at Zvornik, you've described being interrogated now, I think, by three people or three sorts of people. Firstly, the man whose name you thought was something like Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. I was visited by three types of people. That's how it was. There were soldiers, officers and policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And to cut matters short, the abuse you received there were from some drunken policemen, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Who is going next? Mr. Ostojic will be cross-examining you and he is counsel for Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a series of questions, I hope not to be repetitive, and I thank you in advance for discussing some of these issues with me. We have gotten to know a little bit of each other because we are smiling back and forth but, obviously, some of these are serious topics and I apologise in advance for having to have you recollect some of these issues and thank you for your patience. Sir, this afternoon, you testified when my learned colleague Mr. Haynes was asking you questions, that the shelling on July 12th, 1995, you were shelled in the morning and ambushed in the evening. Do you remember that? Maybe I could help you. It's not a trick question. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him recollect and try to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it's just that the question is unclear to me, because we were shelled on two occasions. This is what is unclear. I don't know what -- which occasion are you referring to, because we were shelled once in the early morning, on the 12th, then we were shelled on the 12th in the evening, except it was in a different place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that and that's the way I understood your statement. In fact, in your statement, if I can just quickly give you the overview that I have, and you correct me if I'm wrong. At 8.30 in the morning, in Buljim, you were ambushed. At 9.30 in Kamenica, there it was an ambush or an attack. And then according to your statement, at 2230 or 10.30 p.m., there was another ambush. And then approximately from 10.30 to midnight on the 12th of July, there was another ambush, whether by shelling or grenade. So four times on the 12th of July 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's all correct. It's just that the times are not correct. When you say in the morning, at 9.30, I think you said, near Buljim, but when you mentioned the second time at 9.30, it was in the evening. So it was at 2030 hours; that's when the second shelling took place. That's what the issue is. The first ambush was near Buljim. There was fierce firing, people were killed there, then they began to shell. I returned to the place where this happened. I was perhaps some 100 -- a few hundred metres ahead, and quite a few of my relatives were left behind, so I went back. And I could see they were bringing in wounded from that area. So I was just asking anyone if they knew the way. In the column, I returned to help those who had been wounded at the rear of the column. I was bringing them out. Of course, when the shelling would subside a little bit, we would move forward. When the shelling began again, then we would go and take shelter. Then we would go back again to get the wounded. Those who had been killed, we left them in a creek and we just covered them with some leaves and branches because you cannot really carry a person's dead body more than a few kilometres. It would be senseless to carry the bodies all the way to Tuzla. I mean, I can explain this to you. It's not a problem. I can tell you how it was in detail, going from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may just put a question to the witness perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It's acceptable what you said and I accept that. Just concretely, at 8.00 in the morning, according to your statement, there was an ambush at Buljim, correct? And I think in your statement also you say that 30 were killed and 45 injured approximately, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then the next ambush or attack that occurred was approximately an hour and a half later in Kamenica, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ambush was in the morning, just below Buljim. Practically the whole day we spent above Kamenica waiting for those who had gone ahead to send an order, whether we would be able to come across and where, at Vlasenica or somewhere else. It doesn't matter. So we were waiting like that until the evening. That's where we were. Towards evening, there was an explosion. I don't know what exploded. Then the shooting began from all directions at us. Probably they discovered that we were there so they opened fire from all directions and there was shelling, and a lot of people were killed there. This happened on the 12th in the evening, perhaps at about 9.30 or something. I didn't have a watch. I know that it was getting dark. It was July so it got dark later. But it was early evening, you could already see some moonlight.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say that lots or many of people were killed at that ambush at Kamenica, in your statement, I recall that you said between 500 to a 1000. Is that still your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall, of what happened, I believe that it is around that figure. I had the opportunity to return to that place, looking for some relatives, to see if they had been wounded, also because of my brother whom I lost there. Then we were looking, using the cigarette lighter and then whoever you would look at, it wasn't that person, it wasn't him, it wasn't him. There were many who were seriously wounded, who couldn't get up, who couldn't move. You could see that they were still alive but they were almost 99 per cent dead people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who other than you were assisting in providing any medical attention to the wounded and can you tell us how many wounded there were, to the best of your estimation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there were more wounded than killed. And you provided the help that you were able to provide, whether you knew somebody or not, and if you were able to carry someone, that's what you did. You carried them for 100 metres, 500 metres, however long you could. Then there were new ambushes. And then people who were carrying these people too got wounded or killed. So that this number of wounded and killed grew. It increased, as we were advancing at each hundred metres or a kilometre. It just kept increasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, at one point in your statement, in connection with this Kamenica ambush, you state that we built stretchers to assist the wounded. And I want to talk to you a little bit about that. Who is the "we" who built the stretchers? You and just all the other men that were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew some people from Bljeceva. That's a village close to where I was. Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whom I knew. And they were carrying a relative of theirs, and as I came up, I helped them to carry this person. While we were carrying him, we covered perhaps 200 metres from the time we set off. And then a man came out from behind a tree with an M53 rifle, and I was familiar with the weapon, and he rushed out and he started shooting at us. All the people who were in front of me, because he fired at us from a distance of perhaps 10 to 20 metres from the right-hand side, they all fell. I fell too. I could just feel hot air all around me, and I thought that I had been wounded also. When the shooting stopped, the person just went back behind that beech tree and went down the slope. I got up. I could see that I was able to walk, but no one else there was able to stand up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I said your statement, sir, in connection with that -- thank you, I don't necessarily need to repeat it. What I needed to know just on that part, during that time, which I have on my notes as being in the evening, sometime -- we won't argue about the time. I know there were -- how many people actually were killed in that ambush that you were the only survivor when the man came with the machine-gun? How many people in that group died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were eight of us altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to just the stretchers, if I may. You mentioned that they were stretchers that were made from the wood and from blankets. I believe in your statement, do you know -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the blankets were tied to the actual wood that you were holding to carry the injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They tied the ends of the blanket, one end to the front end and the other side to the back end and there were two poles that were used. That's how they tied that together.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the technique where you can strip a collar off or a sleeve of someone and then use it as a knot to tie the blanket to a pole or a wood to make it into a makeshift stretcher? Are you familiar with that technique at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, I'm familiar with that technique, but there was no time to use it. All there was time for was to tie it as soon as possible and to get out there. You would need more time to use that technique than you needed to just tie the both ends to the poles.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just share with me, sir. You learned this technique based on your military training and experience, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where did you learn that technique?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I come from the country. I'm a man from the village. If I were from the town, perhaps I wouldn't have known this technique.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and turn to another topic. That is, you mention in your statement, late midnight the 12th of July 1995, you noticed that there was strange behaviour within the group or column of men that you were with and there were suicides that were being committed. Do you remember that at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you also say in your statement that they were shooting each other. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you estimate for us, to the best of your recollection, how many suicides were there and how many people actually shot at each other or ultimately killed each other within the group that you were with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This all happened after the second shelling, below the Kamenicko Brdo, Kamenica hill. It was in the direction of a village called Suljici. After that shelling, I was able to see something like that. I actually had the opportunity to see that on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Both at that same place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where was that other place that that occurred, suicides and people turning arms against one another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened at a hill above the village that I mentioned. I think the name of the village is Suljici. So it was on that hill. People behaved strangely. They were sleepy. Anything you would say to them, the people would listen to you. If you were to tell them, go this way, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I heard the other area. It was both then within that mountainous area called Suslici [phoen], correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suljici.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And both of those incidences that you experienced with the suicide and the men or people turning arms against each other, both happened in and around that area, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not both.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just below.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I just get an answer -- I'll move on, Your Honour. I can move on on this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a problem at all. Perhaps some two or three kilometres approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just if I may ask one question on this just to wrap it up, Your Honour. Sir, just estimate for us, if you can, how many people in your estimation that you saw died of suicide and/or by killing each other within the groups that they were with by turning arms on each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw two such cases. In one, one person killed another. In the other case, I don't know whether you could consider that to be suicide, because the person killed two -- four more people. I just wanted to explain a little bit about that, and it's all in my statement. When this shelling was going on, and then when it stopped, this second shelling, we tried to rush through and there were large or big clouds of smoke because of this shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have that in your statement and I apologise for cutting you off. So I don't want to repeat it, but thank you for that. I was just curious, because in the statement, it didn't have the precise number and I needed your help on that.
