The next point, if I can have your assistance on -- and that is the area of Konjevic Polje, on the 13th of July 1995, you mentioned, I believe, previously, that that's where most or the greatest amount of people actually died as a result of gunfire or battles or ambushes, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the people who were surrendering or --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, because I think you testified that -- about that already in Sandici earlier and we have your testimony and your statement on that. I'm talking about the ambush that occurred on the 13th of July 1995 at Konjevic Polje. Was there an ambush there when the column was trying to go through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a little bit confused by the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The dates, let me just maybe help you with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two things. It has happened already more than once during your cross-examination, Mr. Ostojic, that you put questions to the witness which more or less arise from what he -- what is included in the statement, in the witness -- so-called witness statements. We would like you, in future, when you do that again, to refer the witness directly to that part and read out to him if necessary the relevant part on which you are basing your questions. That's the first thing. And the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On for that purpose, I think since we -- this is only the second in the line of cross-examinations, and we don't have previous testimony of this witness, but we have his witness statements. I think they should be made available to him while you are examining him. The third thing is addressed to you. If you are getting tired, do let us know and we will stop. Or if you require a break, do let us know and we'll have a break. In the meantime, Madam Registrar, if we could procure a hard copy of the statements and have them at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose the B/C/S version. I don't know that he understands English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was just trying to speed the process up and I apologise to the Court for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that but as you know we look at things with a completely different pair of spectacles.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was -- fair enough, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you will find no objection to do that. Yes, I think the witness wants to tell us something. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for all of that. I would just like to say one thing to you: A gentlemen put this question to me about the ambush, when I was ambushed. I came across several ambushes, so I don't which one he was referring to. I would be glad to answer but I would just like to know what ambush the question was related to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you. That's more than fair. And I thought I was referring to the ambush that I believe you mentioned in your statement is in Konjevic Polje and I will find that for you. I'm not sure if the witness has his statement yet with him.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Is it e-court Exhibit 63 maybe?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe the Prosecutor tendered the exhibit into evidence, so we are relying on that tender therefore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we would like the witness to have is exactly P02288, in hard copy. I don't want the witness to be scrolling up and down. If the Prosecution can provide a copy, if that is easier, just make sure that it is shown to the Defence before it is handed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe we do have a copy available for the witness's inspection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Show it to Mr. Ostojic so that he's satisfied that it's the right document. All right? Thank you. So witness, any time -- witness -- witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time you wish to pause and check the relevant part of a statement to which you are being addressed, please do so, by all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do tell us as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I shall. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me direct your attention first to the second page of that statement after your general background information. And it's under paragraph number 5. Just to recap quickly, I think under paragraph number 5 it states that the same day, the 12th July 1995, at about 8 -- "08:00 the column was ambushed." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that was the ambush that was below the hill of Buljim, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then immediately after that, you talk about another ambush that happened at the crossroads of Konjevic Polje and Kravica. In the same paragraph, shortly there after, I think you give an estimate of how many kilometres you walked, approximately three. I think it's in your statement, if I can just have you look there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think what Mr. Ostojic is referring to is the road that runs between Konjevic Polje and Kravica. I don't believe that there is an indication it was in the crossroads or an intersection or anything of that nature. But that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll read the exact thing, Your Honour. Shortcuts sometime take longer. Thank you for that. If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the best way to. This is what we suggested actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It says here in the fifth paragraph of your statement, "This is the road which runs between Konjevic Polje and Kravica." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And would that, sir, be the second ambush that you experienced, on that date, the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th of July, that's when the first ambush took place, below Buljim, as it says here, near Bare. That was the first ambush. The second shooting, well, ambush, whatever you may think it is, happened in the evening, above Kamenica, around 9.30 approximately. Then, well, there were a few ambushes, from Kamenicko Brdo, where the second ambush took place, one, two, three times, up until the asphalt road. It happened three times. It happened when we were carrying the wounded person. That was the third time. And then moving further on from there, 200, 300, 500 metres approximately, doesn't matter, but all of that through the woods, over this meadow, where we reached an ambush yet again. When we moved to the right, there was an ambush there and quite a few people got killed. As we went back, these 200, 300, 400 metres back, as we were discussing where we would go and what we would do, gunfire came from our left-hand side. Again people got killed there. And then we walked down the slope a bit to the right, through these big ferns. To our right, were some houses that had been burned. Now, were there Muslim or Serb, I don't know. As we were running down the meadows, shelling started. Then I lay there, down on the road. When I felt this strange smoke, I told people to get their T-shirts wet or whatever else they had to put it on their mouths. I was wondering whether it was some kind of poisonous gas or something. Many people did that. Many people around me. My brother was there. As we went on from there, when the shelling stopped, again we got up and we went further down. As we ran from there, at that moment, a shell came, a shell fell there, in front of one of my neighbours. Right by him perhaps. Threw him into the ferns, a few metres. I thought that he must have been totally dismembered but after a while, the man got up, and he said, to me, "Do you think that I'm all swollen?" And I said, "No, you're fine, you're quite normal." And the man behaved in a very strange way as we were there together, perhaps due to the detonation, the explosion or whatever. I have no idea, was it the smoke? Was it fear? Was it all of it? As we were running, in a column, further down, as we were passing by this field and we got into the woods, perhaps only about 10 metres or so, and then further down, there are some rocks, and then you go right down to the river. Just as we were getting into the woods, there were two men on the right side, two men on the left side. They had weapons in their hands, and they were saying, "Faster, faster," to us. When the last one got there, as people were running in front of me, he slipped and fell into the river. I planned to hold on to a branch, a tree branch because I saw people sliding into the river. As I was holding on to this tree, I heard some noise. I turned around, these people who were standing on the two sides caught the last one who got there. This man did not have a rifle. And he was saying, "Let me go, let me go." I just heard them say, "Slaughter him, fuck his mother." When I heard all of that I let the branch go, and as I let the branch go, a bomb exploded. A grenade exploded. And when I saw what happened to the rest, I jumped and I fled from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, thank you for that answer. Let me just generally ask you, if I may, sir, from the time that you left Susnjari on the 11th in the evening up until the time of your capture, whether it's the 18th or 19th, or whatever day it is, just that date, those three or five days, is it your testimony -- or am I correct, sir, that you experienced these ambushes and this gunfire that was happening each and every day? Each and every day the men in your column were being shot at and killed; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you estimate to the best of your recollection, sir, while you were with your column walking through the woods or the trek that you took to try to get to the free territory, you also saw dead corpses on the road; correct? During that five or whatever period time it is, from Susnjari up until the time that you were -- that you surrendered. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And those were people who had been killed prior to the ambushes that you experienced; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So your part of the column experienced ambushes, and it's likely or reasonable, at least to you, that the men or the column before you also experienced some ambushes on that same road or trail or however we can describe that; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. At all these places, there were ambushes. My column and columns consisting of other people, I mean the column that I was in, it was never the same column that I had left Susnjari in. I always came across these other people, and then when we would get to an ambush, then some people would get killed and then others would run away, and then we would meet up with people from other columns. And they kept changing, if I can put it that way. We met people, other people, we were never in the same column. Because if we were all moving in one column, I mean, had we been able to move in one column, it would mean that we would have all gotten killed. I wouldn't have had anyone else to go along with. So it was always different, somebody lost somebody else, and then somebody else would meet up with yet other people, so, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Two very minor points, if you could help clarify for me, sir. When you were going back and assisting the wounded in this column, isn't it true that the majority of them had suffered gunshot wounds and that was the cause of their death? To the best of your ability.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were quite a few people whose throats got slit, who had been wounded. I personally did not see people doing that but I heard from other people, when we would meet up in a column, as you were changing these columns, you know. I mean, you would run away and then you would meet other people, you would meet these people, and somebody would say, I saw with my very own eyes how they were going behind the last people who were moving from Srebrenica. I mean, from Buljim, from Kamenica, from Konjevic Polje, never mind. But as I said, from Srebrenica, towards Tuzla, the last people who were moving along saw all sorts of things happening. And they saw that these were Chetniks who were cleaning up the terrain. They were killing, slaughtering the wounded. They saw that with their very own eyes. I'm not talking in my own name. I'm talking about these people who told me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your honest answer and helping us here. All I wanted to know is that if you saw any gunshot wound victims there. But let me ask you this: During the five-day period or so from the time that you left Susnjari to go to the free territory up until the time you surrendered, can you estimate for us to the best of your ability how many men died as a result of these ambushes or fire-fights that you experienced on your trek to Tuzla or Nezuk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Srebrenica to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Once the column was formed and thereafter up until the time of your surrender, that which you personally experienced and that which you saw personally, the corpses as you've described for us in your statement, do you estimate that the number is, what, I hate to put a number to you but -- I'm asking you, inviting you to give me a number.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could say a formal figure, even if I had been counting, I wouldn't have dared to say anything in terms of an exact figure. Well, maybe -- well, let me put it this way: I came across some seriously wounded people who could not move. So quite simply, a person could count them as dead. And there were others who were actually dead. At least 1500.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. And good luck.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Who is next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic is defending Mr. Nikolic in this case and she will be cross-examining you next. I don't know if you know, Ms. Nikolic, but you have been assigned a temporary co-counsel to assist you, so he will be most welcome. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it possible to get an estimate so that we can let the witness go if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I think we have another 12 minutes now and then three-quarters of an hour, so you will be cross-examining the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I will finish by the break. I need about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe I will have any significant cross-examination, perhaps just two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes or so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So hopefully we should be able to make it with this witness after the break, by the end of today's sitting. So -- but, however, the next witness, if he happens to be here, you can send him home. By "home" I mean send him to the hotel. All right. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put a few questions to you related to period after the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you help me with the document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry for [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified in great detail today that after the 21st [realtime transcript read in error "12th"] of July with a group of 39 persons you were transferred to the north to -- near the village of Batkovic to a camp for POWs in the territory of the municipality of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In addition to your own group, there were other prisoners or detainees coming in from Srebrenica, Vlasenica and so on, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move into private session because we are going to refer to some names in this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go into private session. We are in private session already. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Who is next? Have you made arrangements amongst yourselves or not? Mr. Zivanovic has already informed the registrar -- the Deputy Registrar that he will not be cross-examining the witness. Mr. Krgovic? Mr. Krgovic is appearing for General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put a few questions to you that are related to the very beginning of your statement and of your testimony. They have to do with your coming to Susnjari. That's going to be the topic that I will be dealing with. You said in your statement, that was admitted into evidence here, in response to the Prosecutor's question, that in the evening on that day, I think it was the 12th of July, sorry, the 11th of July --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: -- that you were ordered to leave the trenches where you were and to go to Susnjari, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you came to Susnjari, when you came to that place, you were in a group together with people from your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want to go into private session? Let's go into private session. I still didn't get the interpretation of what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I said let's go back to open session. But that seems to be according to the transcript a response to your request to go into private session. While we were already in private session. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the problem is when I said, "Let's go back to open session," I said that in English, and because I was overlapping with the English translation, it did not go into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's okay. I just wanted for the record to explain that we are not two crazy persons, one saying exactly the opposite of what he should be saying. So let's continue in open session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, from what I understood from your statement, you were at the rear of the column; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rear, meaning it's in the front or in the back?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It means to be in the back.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I was not in the back of the column. I was somewhere in between. There were a lot of people. The column was very long. In order to go through Buljim -- through a crossing in Buljim, where that section was mined, we had to go one by one past that place. So the column was kilometres long. So even though, even if I was in the front of the column, I was just one amongst hundreds and thousands of people, so I still wasn't at the front. So I was somewhere between the middle and the front. It's a little bit hard now to decide, to say. It's hard to say that I was in front. It would be another thing if there were only 20 of us. Then I would be able to say that I was in the front or in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So are you trying to say that your position in the column changed as it was moving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The unit that was next to you or that was behind you, was that the mountain battalion under the command of Ejub Golic at the time when the column was formed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It makes it possible for us to have the break here. We did not have any redactions? No. So we now have Mr. Lazarevic again, Madam Fauveau, and that's it. All right. We can have a 30-minute -- 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have practically two questions for you relating to actually a qualification or a clarification of what you said today. The first question has to do with the people who took you from the place where you were captured, who took you to the village, and then after that who took to you Zvornik. Today, on two occasions, you said you were taken away by police officers. Did you think of military police officers? This is what you said in your statement -- paragraph 12, first sentence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it would be smart to move to private session because the answer the witness gave to Mr. Krgovic and my questions are related to these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lazarevic has concluded his cross-examination and Madam Fauveau for General Miletic is about to start her cross-examination and has asked to go into private session. So let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Today you said this was on page 24, lines 11 to 16, you had received an order whereby you should not resist the Serbs because your family was in Potocari. When you had decided, I mean the people living in the enclave of Srebrenica, when you decided to leave for Susnjari, under the command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you knew you had to cross Serb lines, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how we could get out of there without crossing Serb lines. I don't know if there was any place where we could pass without Serb lines being there. Excuse me. If there was such a place somewhere, where we could pass without it being a Serb line, that we could pass across safely, then very well, but I know 1.000 per cent, not just me, but all the gentlemen here, that no such place existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If you had received the order not to resist the Serbs and you needed to cross Serb lines, why did you just not simply surrender to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I had occasion to see with my own eyes people surrendering without a single shot being fired, and these people were executed right there in cold blood, meaning that if we had surrendered, all of us at that time, then, as you say, we would all have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Why did you not go to Potocari with your relatives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have gone there, and I would have -- would have met the same fate as those 3.000 who had been picked, ranging from three years of age and up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Today you said, this was on page 30, line 12 to 16, that you had been betrayed by the United Nations. Did you feel also betrayed by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is quite a question, but I will respond. As for the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would not involve it here. As for the United Nations, and the rest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... about United Nations and the rest. I think you can safely go to the next question, Madam Fauveau. I don't see any relevance in what he thinks about the Bosnian government's role in all this. It's not the Bosnian government that is being tried here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You said that the United Nations had betrayed you because Srebrenica was a safe area. Is it true that Srebrenica was to be a safe area and a demilitarised area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it already was a safe area, and you're asking the question of should it have been a safe zone. As far as I know, it was a safe zone, according to all of the Geneva Conventions. Unfortunately, what happened happened, and others can judge who should bear the responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, is it right that Srebrenica was to be a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify that word, "Demilitarised"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Prosecution, do you contest this, that it was supposed to be because I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think it's pretty clear what this was. It was what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Finished. Stop. Stop there. There is no argument that it should have been demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that there is no argument to state that it had been demilitarised. Maybe I can just ask the question or maybe the Prosecution would like to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I will not involve the Prosecution in that but you can ask the question, because I think if you look at the adjudicated facts, you already find quite some material on this, which has -- any way, if you think that that is not correct, you have every right to contest it but I think amongst the adjudicated facts, you have already an acknowledgement that the situation on the ground was far from what demilitarisation meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Your Honour. I withdraw my question and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Is there re-examination, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, there is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just have one question. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you were captured, you mentioned at one stage that one of the soldiers or officers that were interrogating you also mentioned your brother.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That both of you would be spared and exchanged if you did something or whatever. How did he know about your brother? Did -- was this something spontaneous on his part or was it you that mentioned the existence of your brother to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-139 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mentioned it first to me and I was really surprised by the fact that he found that out, and how he found it out. It's my opinion that the person, and I don't know if I am permitted to say his name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that brings your testimony to an end ^ here. You will be assisted to facilitate your journey back home. On behalf of everyone, I wish to thank you for having come over and also I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, documents, exhibits? Mr. Vanderpuye? I think we have only got one or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, in addition to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not the statement. That has already been given a number, 2288.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've got nothing else?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, it's just the pseudonym sheet and the prior statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But those are already admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. 7D63, page 5, which is the sheet containing four military insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not certain exactly what it's being offered for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being offered because the witness was shown those insignia and initially he said it wasn't like that. So if it wasn't like that, at least we will have evidence of what it wasn't like. Then we also have a specimen of the eagle and he agreed that the eagle was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's admitted and marked, I don't know what number. Madam Fauveau, you made use of --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Could 3D17 please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And this will be kept under seal. There is no objection, I take it, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is no objection, but there is a matter of clarification, because when the witness was shown that document, he referred to a name that was positioned on the third line down on page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can I go to private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before we adjourn, I notice Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. I'd completely fallen asleep and Mr. Ostojic turned around to remind me that there was something that we collectively wish to raise. The question of the distribution of proofing notes came to our attention following a remark of Judge Kwon's yesterday, which made it apparent to us that these documents are being circulated to everybody. And in our view, they ought not to be circulated to the Bench. It was particularly relevant in this case, because what was said in the proofing note in relation to this witness, did not in fact become a matter of his testimony, and so documents are being circulated to you, the Tribunal of fact, that are -- that are, in our view, not properly put before you. I don't think this is a contentious issue because we did raise it with the Prosecution during one of the breaks today and it looks as though it's simply a case of somebody having a circular e-mail address that includes too many addresses. But we did want to raise that collectively now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that I think this is the first proofing notes that we have received since we started in August. To be frank with you, I thought there would be special reason for it, which ultimately never emerged. I speak for myself. I am not interested in proofing notes. And although there is no hard and fast rule here what the Bench should receive and what it shouldn't receive, there are other Chambers, as you are aware, that insist on having all previous statements of witnesses made available to the Judges, proofing notes made available to the Judges. We have not adopted that system here. You know where we come from. And we are not interested, unless that becomes an issue. Unless the witness says no, it's not true, I never said that while I was being proofed. You know, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in any case, I mean, I am not interested in them, but since the practice in this Tribunal varies, I wouldn't impose my preference on any of the other three Judges in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's probably something we don't need your help on at this stage. We can sort it out between ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the position. And I think we've discussed this before and there is no interest that I know of from anyone of us to have proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask that in this case, the evidence-in-chief was introduced in part by -- in the form of written statements. What harm there would be in receiving the supplement of the written statement? So this is not in strict terms a proofing note.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, a further statement. The difficulty I suppose with a proofing note is, and I didn't explore it with this witness, although it was in my mind to do so, is you don't actually know whether he's approved the proofing note. The proofing note is a document created by those who sit down and talk to him and summarise what they say they've talked to him about. And it may very well be that were the witness to look at that proofing note, he'd say actually, that doesn't reflect what I was saying. And it doesn't bear any signature of his and it doesn't bear any acknowledgement by him that it's an accurate reflection of what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to discuss this any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't, but out of courtesy, I answered the question. We can sort it out between us. We don't need your help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can sort it out. And what I would like to point out, for example, that rather than having this, I would agree completely with you that if there are supplementary -- if there is supplementary information to the written statement, that should come from the horse's mouth, from the witness's mouth, and not indirectly prior -- previously from the Prosecution itself. I mean, going through this, for example, I do notice that there are some statements mentioned in this document that the witness never repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there is one further reason in my mind why I wouldn't like to receive these. But that's again my position, and I have taken this position in previous cases, but I also left free the other Judges that were composing the Trial Chamber with me to show another preference, and it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I may address the issue. And I did explain to Defence counsel earlier that I am actually the one who is responsible for distributing these proofing notes and I did so Sunday night, I believe it was. And there was nobody really around to make the policy determination as to where they should go at the time that I distributed them. And I copied the Court. I just copied the court with the documents that had been disclosed with the Defence, to the Defence. It was not an intent to -- with any intent to kind of influence the Court in any way improperly and I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that ever crossed our mind, either then or now, Mr. Vanderpuye. I mean, so, please, don't worry about this. But you -- now it has been raised and you know what our preference or our position is more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you kindly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I leave everyone free to take a different approach if that is so desired. So we will adjourn until tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
